In the time before time, when the world was young and formless, there lived a spider named Arachnis who dwelled in the space between waking and sleeping. Unlike ordinary spiders, Arachnis spun webs not of silk, but of pure thought and imagination.

Each night, as humans closed their eyes, Arachnis would climb down from her celestial perch and begin her sacred work. With eight legs moving in perfect harmony, she wove intricate patterns in the darkness—each strand a different dream. Golden threads became adventures of courage and triumph. Silver strands transformed into memories of loved ones long passed. Dark purple fibers carried warnings and lessons the dreamer needed to learn.

But Arachnis grew lonely in her eternal task. One night, she wove a special dream—a vision of another weaver who could share her burden. When the first human dreamer awakened and remembered this dream, they picked up needle and thread, creating the first tapestry.

This is why, even today, we say that artists and storytellers "weave tales" and "spin yarns." They are the children of Arachnis, continuing her ancient work, transforming the invisible threads of imagination into something the waking world can touch and treasure.

Each fragment caught the light of distant stars and began to dance across the sky, shimmering in brilliant greens, purples, and blues. The Sky Weaver was enchanted. She gathered the remaining threads of starlight and wove them into great curtains that would ripple and wave across the northern heavens.

From that night forward, whenever people gathered in darkness to share warmth and stories, the Sky Weaver would unfurl her luminous tapestries across the sky as a gift—a reminder that even in the deepest cold and longest nights, beauty and wonder persist.

The people named this phenomenon the aurora borealis, but they never forgot it was the Sky Weaver's tears of joy, frozen and transformed into eternal light.
